Chapter 9. The Evolution of Spiritual Abstraction
As the twentieth century rolled in, the search for spiritual meaning in art started to evolve in some pretty unexpected ways. Suddenly, those old boundaries between genres and disciplines? They just began to blur. Painters found themselves inspired by music, writers borrowed ideas from dance, and sculptors even drew from poetry.
The result was a burst of fresh styles and approaches, each one chasing the impossible—to express what can’t quite be put into words.
Some artists dove headfirst into pure abstraction, letting go of anything that pointed back to the visible world. Their canvases turned into open fields of color and light—a kind of space where you could just stop and wonder. Others played with symbolism, weaving shapes and signs into their work to hint at realities that sit just beneath the surface.
And then there were those who mixed up abstraction and figuration, giving us art that danced somewhere between the familiar and the completely unknown.
For a lot of these artists, these choices weren’t just about style—they were about something deeper. They were searching for a bridge, a way for art to connect the material with the immaterial, the seen with the unseen. By letting go of strict representation, they hoped to tap into those powerful undercurrents of feeling and thought that just can’t be shown directly.
Picture this: a sculptor who’s spent years carving stone, suddenly decides to experiment with light and shadow. The new work is delicate, almost fleeting—something a camera could never really capture. At first, the sculptor is worried people won’t get it, maybe even dismiss it as too insubstantial. But over time, it becomes clear that its very impermanence is what makes it so powerful. It gently asks you to slow down, to really pay attention, and to experience the present moment in an entirely new way.
Most people don’t realize just how much of modern art has been shaped by this search for spiritual abstraction. Think about the bold colors in one painting, the stark simplicity in another, or the playful rhythms of a third. All of them are reaching beyond what you see at first glance—they’re trying to create a sense of mystery and awe.
And you know what? This evolution is still happening. Every new generation finds fresh ways to explore the spiritual side of art—using new materials, new ideas, and new technologies. Sure, the forms may shift, but that deep urge remains: to create art that speaks to the soul, that invites us to see both the world and ourselves with completely fresh eyes.
